newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-many seen just above EMU debt threshold.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-many seen just above EMU debt threshold.

text.p: The European Commission, in a review of Germany's economic convergence programme for monetary union, sees outstanding government debt hovering just above 60.0 percent of GDP in 1997, a source said on Thursday.

Countries wishing to join economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 must have their debt level "sufficiently diminishing" and approaching the Maastricht treaty's reference value of 60 percent of total output.
For 1998 and 1999, the EU executive expects Bonn's debt level to range between 60.5 and 61.0 percent and decline by 0.5 percentage points in the year 2000.
One of the major worries about Germany's ability to meet the preconditions of EMU has been a recent tendency for its debt level to rise.

A Reuter poll released on Thursday showed a vast majority of analysts expecting EMU to be launched on schedule in 1999, but their optimism has dimmed somewhat due to doubts about Germany's ability to strictly adhere to the Maastricht targets.
Record unemployment levels in Germany and the consequent impact on Bonn's finances have been at the root of their concerns, prompting speculation that EMU might have to be postponed beyond 1999.
EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy, however, reaffirmed on Thursday the political committment to launch Europe's single currency on time.
"There is no question about changing the criteria or changing the date," de Silguy told a briefing of Swedish jounalists.
In assessing Germany's programme the Commission expressed its own doubts about a rapid reduction in unemployment.
"The Commission says that unemployment will be reduced less rapidly than expected," the source said.
There was no specific comment on Bonn's projected budget deficit of 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997.
Convergence programmes for both Germany and France will top the agenda of a meeting of EU finance ministers on Monday.
EU diplomats on Thursday predicted both plans would be viewed favourably by the bloc's 15 members.
"There is general agreement that German economic policies...are going in the right direction," said one diplomat.
Regarding France, the Commission praised French efforts to reduce its budget deficit and the introduction of measures to keep expenditure under tight control.
But it doubted whether French economic growth projections of 2.5 percent in real GDP over the next few years could be attained.
"There is a risk that projected growth of 2.5 percent between 1998 and 2001 could not be attained," the source added.
France's convergence plan extends to the year 2001 while Germany's runs up to 2000.
The Commission, however, was optimistic that France could meet its projected budget deficit of 3.0 percent of GDP for 1997, the critical year for meeting the preconditions for monetary union.

"It's likely that the target will be achieved...given the economic growth forecasts and the discretionary measures announced," the source said. The Commission noted, however, there was a risk on both the revenue and expenditure side.
The Commission also said that beyond 1998 the French programme envisages a decline in the budget deficit to just above 1.0 percent of total output.
